title: Joseph and the Seven Years of Plenty
text:
Pharaoh had two dreams in one night. In the first, seven fat, healthy cows came up out of the Nile, followed by seven gaunt, ugly cows, which ate the fat ones. In the second, seven full ears of grain grew on one stalk, and then seven thin ears, scorched by the east wind, swallowed them up. None of Egypt's wise men could explain the dreams.

Then Pharaoh's chief cupbearer remembered a young Hebrew he had met in prison, who had correctly explained his own dream. Joseph was brought out, shaved and dressed, and stood before Pharaoh. It was not in him, he said, but God would give Pharaoh an answer. The two dreams were one: seven years of great plenty were coming to Egypt, followed by seven years of famine so severe that the plenty would be forgotten.

Then he gave advice. Pharaoh should appoint a wise and discerning man over the land, set officials to collect a fifth of the harvest during the good years, and store the grain in the cities as a reserve for the famine.

Pharaoh put Joseph himself in charge. For seven years he gathered grain until it was like the sand of the sea and they stopped measuring it. When the famine came and spread across all lands, there was bread in Egypt, and people from every country came there to buy grain.
lesson: Good years are when you prepare for bad ones. Set aside a fixed share in times of plenty, before you need it, because when the famine comes, it is too late to start saving.
caveat: The story belongs to the patriarchal narratives of Genesis, whose historicity is not established by outside evidence.
